narrative: On 18 August 2025, a team was installing a 6-inch pipe over a 35-metre section between two lines. This pipe was also to be used during WO operations. During the operation, the team separated a 6-inch pipe from a 2-inch pipe, both of which had previously been tied together with cords. When the third cord was cut, the tension accumulated in the 6-inch pipe, which was bent at the time, was suddenly released. The pipe rebounded and struck an operator's right leg between the ankle and knee, causing an open fracture. The supervisor was immediately informed, the control room was alerted, and emergency procedures were quickly implemented.

narrative: On January 19, 2025, during restart attempts of the HP-A Gas Compressor following corrective maintenance, an unusually loud noise was heard from the exhaust. Seconds later, the fire alarm was triggered, and it was observed that the exhaust structure had fallen off. Technicians in the vicinity immediately pressed the compressor’s emergency stop button and evacuated the facility. Simultaneously, the emergency response team was activated, and the on-scene commander initiated a full facility shutdown using a manual call point near the compressor building. Once the source of the loud noise was confirmed to be the HP-A compressor, with the exhaust lying on the ground, the area was cordoned off, and an investigation was launched. The compressor was manually shut down, and the ESD-1 emergency stop was activated.

narrative: During a heavy rainstorm, two aluminium composite panels (component of the external cladding material for the Office building) dislodged and dropped. The two (2) panels, each weighing 9.8kgs and measuring 1.11x1.49ms, dropped from about a height of 22.35 meters. The fallen panels were found Infront of the South Wing Power room, and the affected area was promptly cordoned off to prevent further hazards. Additionally, multiple panels were observed hanging loosely, posing a potential safety risk to occupants and visitors.
what_went_wrong: 1. Aluminium composite panels not airtight. - Previous investigations revealed that no consideration was given to the potential for panels falling during design and installation. Furthermore, subsequent structural integrity assessments did not clearly establish the mode of failure and effective mitigation measures to prevent recurrence. Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel. 2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained. Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
corrective_actions: 1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term. 2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.

narrative: At about 02:21hrs, while rig crew was picking 4” drill pipe, a single drill pipe was picked from Catwalk to the rig floor with Air winch tugger. The IP removed thread protector from the single pipe while another floorman attempted to guide the pipe into the mouse hole. The pipe missed the mouse hole, hit the rig floor and also hit the IP on his right ear and shoulder. IP was move to Clinic.
what_went_wrong: 1. Lowering without signal – The air tugger operator lowered the pipe without receiving a stop/lower command, due to absence of a dedicated signaller and reliance on previous experience racking 11 stands without one. 2. Obstructed line of sight – The operator was blindsided by the position of already-racked pipes, limiting visibility of the mousehole area. 3. IP in fall zone – The injured person was inadvertently in the trajectory of the falling pipe after removing the thread protector. 4. Incoherent communication – The floormen recognized the pipe had missed the mousehole but were only able to shout warnings, which were not effectively received
corrective_actions: 1. Updating and endorsing the racking SOP. 2. Assigning a dedicated signaller for all pipe-handling operations. 3. Adjusting derrick camera positioning to restore clear line of sight. 4. Reinforcing communication protocols and hazard-zone controls.

No personnel were struck; however, dropped-object energy indicated fatality potential. The plate was originally installed as a dropped-object prevention measure. narrative: At approximately 06:30, lifting operations were being conducted to move spools from the main deck to the cellar/ sub-cellar deck. Because no direct lifting path existed, the crew chose to lift the load through a slickline hatch, which constituted a complex lift and was not covered by the approved PTW. The crane operator had no line of sight and was communicating by radio only. During lifting, the hook snagged the hatch plate. The rigger, who was standing on the hatch cover to guide the load, attempted to stop the lift. The plate dislodged and the rigger fell approximately 6.5 m to the deck below. The injured person was medevaced with serious injuries. The event had clear fatality potential.
what_went_wrong: • A complex lifting operation was performed under a PTW that only authorised a standard lift. • Work scope changed without risk assessment or lift planning. • Crane operator had no line of sight and communications were unreliable. • Rigger stood on the hatch cover to guide the load, placing himself in a fall hazard zone. • The lift was coordinated using voice/radio in a noisy area without clear signalling control. • Rigger’s certification had expired and supervision was inadequate. • Unsafe practice had become normalised due to prior similar lifts performed without incident.
corrective_actions: • Complex lifts require a specific lift plan, risk assessment, and supervision. • Never route loads through hatches/openings without engineered lifting arrangements. • Maintain line of sight or use a designated trained signalman with agreed communication protocol. • Personnel must never stand on removable covers or under suspended loads. • Verify competency and certification of riggers and lifting personnel. • Stop work when lift conditions differ from the approved plan.

narrative: While parking the starboard (STBD) crane following routine lifting operations, the crane boom was brought down into the boom rest abruptly rather than in a controlled manner. This sudden placement generated an unexpected impact load on the crane structure, producing a loud bang that was heard in the vicinity of the crane pedestal and surrounding areas. The securing equipment should be as short as practically possible. • The area below must always be sufficiently cordoned off. 28

narrative: On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60–90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
what_went_wrong: The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
corrective_actions: Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high- risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight. narrative: Collision between northern crane and derrick resulting in falling objects.
what_went_wrong: Three objects fell after the north crane collided with the derrick. The crane operator had been planning to perform lubrication of the slewing ring with the logistics discipline responsible for some time, but this was changed to the crane operator bringing along a deck operator who was being trained as a crane-operator. A helicopter was on its way to the platform, and they had about 25 minutes to finish before the helicopter arrived. It was decided that the crane operator was to perform the lubrication in the crane pedestal while the deck operator operated the crane. The crane was lifted and swung out over the sea. The crane operator reminded to "elevate the crane-boom" to avoid the derrick and then went down into the pedestal. The deck operator elevated the boom and swung the crane towards the platform. After a brief stop to change the lubrication cartridge, the crane was topped up a little more before it swung further towards the derrick. The deck operator believed the boom was topped up enough. The walkway and the spotlight mounted on the right side of the boom were driven into the upper corner of the wind wall high up in the derrick. At the same time, the crane was lifted somewhat and detached from the tower. The crane shook, and the deck operator observed an object fall into an area where personnel were normally present. After receiving information about what had happened over the radio, the crane operator came to the cabin, took over, and lowered the crane into the cradle. The logistics discipline responsible heard what was being said on the radio, responded, and found the spotlight in a pallet with wooden lids in the moonpool area. A section of weather protection from the derrick was found a few minutes later, and a bracket for securing electrical cables was found three days later on a walkway one level above the moonpool area.
corrective_actions: • Use of anti-collision systems on offshore cranes. • Certified safety training for crane operators. • A forum should be established where instructors and trainees can share experiences during the training process. • The management on installations that have personnel undergoing crane operator training should be informed and make this more visible within the organization.

narrative: Two personnel experienced symptoms of severe oxygen deficiency during inspection work, but managed to self- evacuate safely. what_went_wrong: The incident was triggered by nitrogen leakage from the seal system, which under normal ventilated conditions is harmless. However, following a planned emergency shutdown (ESD) and blackstart prior to shutdown period, key barriers were unavailable: ventilation remained off, and the fire dampers which require manual reopening, stayed closed. Without airflow, oxygen was gradually displaced overnight creating a hazardous atmosphere that posed a serious risk of unconsciousness and fatality.

Revise PTW requirements for entries into the turbine enclosure during or after special operational states (e.g., blackstart, shutdown, or loss of HVAC). The PTW must account for potential atmospheric changes, with mandatory portable gas measurements under such conditions.

narrative: During preparations for installing a 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
what_went_wrong: The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with no effective barrier against dropped objects.
corrective_actions: All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier (e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project- wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

narrative: During the night shift, the crew attempted to release an anchor latch tool from a permanent packer using a straight pull of 60 klbs (including 55 klbs string weight) without success. Following contractors’ procedures, the string was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on contractors’ instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site. During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.
what_went_wrong: 1. Uncontrolled rotation using a power tong led to the tubing connection backing off. 2. Thread make-up integrity was not sufficient for rotation under tension. 3. Lack of appropriate equipment (power swivel) resulted in the use of a higher-risk alternative. 4. Dropped-object controls were inadequate, allowing heavy equipment to fall from height.
corrective_actions: 1. Management of Change (MoC) must be applied before deviation. Any deviation from approved procedures, tooling, or operating limits shall be formally reviewed, risk-assessed, and approved through the MBPS MoC process prior to execution. 2. Operations must stop when normal operating parameters are exceeded. When loads, methods, or equipment differ from the original plan, supervisors must stop work and reassess using approved Operator procedures and MoC requirements. 3. Contractually required equipment must be available and used as intended. Operations shall not proceed unless all contract-specified rig equipment is present, functional, and fit for purpose. Temporary or partial substitutions are not acceptable. 4. Stop Work Authority (SWA) must be actively exercised and enforced. All personnel are required to stop work when unsafe conditions exist, including dropped-object exposure, lack of secondary retention, or use of non-approved tools or methods. 5. Secondary retention is mandatory for elevated components. All elevated or moving tools and components shall be secured with secondary retention wherever practicable to prevent dropped-object incidents. 6. Roles and scopes of work must be clearly understood and respected. MIDDLE EAST ONSHORE 41 Operators and service providers shall operate strictly within their defined scopes of work, with no overreach beyond assigned responsibilities.

Reinforce the requirement carefully considering attachment points for fall arrest equipment. 3. Ensure that fall arrest equipment is inspected and certified as per Company Procedure. 4. narrative: On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was released from hospital the same day.
what_went_wrong: The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
corrective_actions: 1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist. 2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible. 3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers. 4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

Safe operation of critical equipment requires clear, shared accountability across suppliers, contractors, and asset owners. Pre-mobilization checks, acceptance inspections, condition monitoring, and post-event inspections must be treated as mandatory control points throughout the equipment lifecycle—not administrative steps.
